data.title: Kernel-Mode Rootkit
data.summary: The sample installs a kernel-mode driver or hooks kernel structures to hide its own files, processes, registry keys or network connections from user-mode tools, including some EDR sensors.
data.description:
Kernel-mode operation gives the rootkit a vantage point above most detection tooling,
which typically runs in user mode: a hidden process simply does not appear in an
enumeration API the kernel component has altered, regardless of how the request was made.
Modern variants frequently abuse a signed, vulnerable third-party driver (a 'bring your own
vulnerable driver' pattern) rather than shipping an unsigned one, to pass driver-signing
enforcement.
data.recommendation:
* Enumerate loaded drivers against a known-good baseline, including version and signer, rather than trusting user-mode process and file listings alone.
* Boot from external/offline media to inspect disk and registry state the live kernel may be hiding.
* Check driver-signing allow-lists for known-vulnerable signed drivers that could be abused to load unsigned code alongside them.
data.short_recommendation: Enumerate loaded drivers against a known-good baseline; do not trust live user-mode listings alone.

mitre_techniques.procedure: Loaded a kernel driver that hooked the process-enumeration syscall table to remove its own PID from returned listings.

mbc_techniques.implementation: Kernel driver hooked NtQuerySystemInformation to filter the sample's own process from enumeration results.
